title: Who Makes the Rules?
bigQuestion: Who should get to make the rules for a whole country, and how should they be chosen?

story.title: Maya Asks a Big Question
story.kicker: Maya reads about people who were not allowed to vote, and she wants to know why.
paragraphs: Maya sat in the school library with a book about the world. One page told about a country long ago. In that country, most people could not vote. One ruler made the laws. People who spoke against him could be put in jail.

Maya frowned. At home, her mom voted every November. Her mom stood in line at the school gym. She filled out a paper ballot. Then she got a sticker that said I Voted. Maya thought everyone in the world did that.

She walked over to Mr. Okafor, the librarian. "Why couldn't those people vote?" she asked. Mr. Okafor smiled. "That is one of the oldest questions there is," he said. "People have argued about it for thousands of years."

He pulled three more books off the shelf. One was about kings and queens. One was about ancient Greece. One was about countries today. "Every country has to decide who makes the rules," he said. "Let's find out how they do it."
story.think: Why do you think a country would let only one person make the laws? What might be good or hard about that?

lessons.title: Making the Rules
lessons.mainIdea: A government is the group that makes and carries out the rules, called laws, for a place.
reading: Think about a crosswalk near your school. Cars must stop when people walk across. That is not just a good idea. It is a rule for everyone. A rule that everyone in a place must follow is called a *law*.

Someone has to write laws and make sure people follow them. That job belongs to the *government*. A government is the group of people who lead a town, a state or a country. Your town, Illinois and the United States each have a government.

Laws help people live together. They tell drivers how fast to go. They say you cannot take what belongs to someone else. Without laws, people might argue over every little thing. Laws give everyone the same rules to follow.

words.d: a rule that everyone in a place must follow
the group of people who lead a town, state or country and make its laws

look.title: A Street With No Rules
look.text: Picture a busy street with no traffic lights, no stop signs and no speed limits. Cars go any way they want. Bikes and walkers try to cross. Nobody knows who should go first.
look.prompt: What problems might happen on this street? Which law would you make first, and why?

check.q: What is a law?
choices: A rule that everyone in a place must follow
A tip that people can ignore
check.why: The reading says a law is a rule that everyone in a place must follow.

check.q: Which group writes laws and makes sure people follow them?
check.why: The reading says the government leads a place and makes its laws.

check.q: Which is an example of a law from the reading?
choices: Wear a red shirt on Monday
Cars must stop for people at a crosswalk
check.why: The reading starts with the crosswalk rule that cars must stop for walkers.

lessons.title: Keeping People Safe
lessons.mainIdea: Governments keep people safe with police, firefighters and courts.
reading: A fire starts in a kitchen on a cold night. Someone calls 911. In a few minutes, a red truck arrives. Firefighters put out the fire. The family is safe. The firefighters work for the city government.

Keeping people safe is one of a government's biggest jobs. *Police* officers help people and make sure laws are followed. Firefighters stop fires. Many governments also have an army to protect the whole country.

Sometimes people disagree about what happened. Did someone break a law? A *court* decides. A court is a place where a judge listens to both sides. Courts help settle problems fairly, without fighting.

words.d: officers who help people and make sure laws are followed
a place where a judge listens to both sides and decides a problem fairly

look.title: Who Would You Call?
look.text: Three things happen in one town. A cat is stuck high in a tree next to smoke from a shed. A bike is stolen from a front yard. Two neighbors disagree about who owns a fence.
look.prompt: For each problem, which government helper might step in: firefighters, police or a court? Explain your choice.

check.q: Who does the reading say arrives to put out a kitchen fire?
check.why: The reading tells how firefighters from the city put out the fire.

check.q: What does a court do?
choices: A judge listens to both sides and decides a problem
check.why: The reading says a court is where a judge listens to both sides and decides.

check.q: Why do courts help a town?
choices: They settle problems fairly without fighting
check.why: The reading says courts help settle problems fairly, without fighting.

lessons.title: Roads, Schools and Taxes
lessons.mainIdea: Governments use tax money to pay for things everyone shares, like roads and schools.
reading: Look at the road outside your school. Who paid to build it? Who fixes the potholes? Most roads are built by a government. So are most public schools, parks and libraries. These are called *public services*.

Public services cost a lot of money. Governments get that money from *taxes*. A tax is money people and businesses pay to the government. When you buy a toy in Illinois, a little extra is added to the price. That extra is a sales tax.

People often disagree about taxes. Some people want lower taxes so families keep more of their money. Others want more services, like new parks, and are willing to pay more. Each place decides this in its own way.

words.d: things a government provides for everyone, like roads, schools and parks
money people and businesses pay to the government

look.title: A Town Budget
look.text: A small town has enough money for one big project this year. The mayor can fix the old bridge, build a new playground or buy a new fire truck. The townspeople have different ideas.
look.prompt: Which project would you choose? What would you say to a neighbor who picked a different one?

check.q: Which of these is a public service?
check.why: The reading names libraries, parks, roads and schools as public services.

check.q: Where do governments get money for public services?
check.why: The reading says a tax is money people and businesses pay to the government.

check.q: What does the reading say about taxes?
choices: People disagree about how high they should be
check.why: The reading explains that some want lower taxes and others want more services.

lessons.title: Ruled by a King or Queen
lessons.mainIdea: In a monarchy, a king or queen rules, and the job usually passes down in one family.
reading: Long ago, France had a king named Louis XIV. He ruled for 72 years, from 1643 to 1715. He built a huge palace at Versailles. He made many big choices for the whole country by himself.

A country ruled by a king or queen is a *monarchy*. The ruler is called a *monarch*. Usually, the job passes from parent to child. A prince or princess may become the next ruler when the old one dies.

Supporters of monarchy said a king gave a country order. Everyone knew who was in charge. Critics said one person should not have so much power. What if the king was unfair? The people could not choose a new one.

words.d: a government ruled by a king or queen
a king or queen who rules a country

look.title: Two Sides of a Crown
look.text: A villager says: "Our queen keeps peace. We know who will rule next, so there are no fights." A second villager says: "But we never got to choose her. If she makes a bad choice, we cannot change it."
look.prompt: What is one good point each villager makes? Which worry seems bigger to you?

check.q: What is a monarchy?
choices: A government ruled by a king or queen
A government where everyone votes on each law
check.why: The reading says a monarchy is a country ruled by a king or queen.

check.q: How does the job of monarch usually pass on?
check.why: The reading says the job usually passes from parent to child.

check.q: What did critics say about monarchy?
choices: One person should not have so much power
check.why: The reading says critics worried one person had too much power and could not be replaced.

lessons.title: The People Choose
lessons.mainIdea: In a democracy, the people choose their leaders or their laws by voting.
reading: Remember Maya's mom? She stood in line and filled out a ballot. A *ballot* is the paper or screen where you mark your choice. Millions of other people did the same that day. Together, they picked their leaders.
A government where the people hold the power is a *democracy*. The word comes from two Greek words. Demos means the people. Kratos means power or rule. So democracy means rule by the people.

In a democracy, people *vote* to make choices. The choice with the most votes usually wins. Leaders who do a poor job can be voted out. Critics note that voting can be slow. People also argue a lot before they decide.

words.d: a government where the people hold power, often by voting
to make a choice, such as picking a leader, that gets counted with others
the paper or screen where a voter marks a choice

look.title: Lincoln Describes Democracy
look.text: "...government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth."
look.prompt: Lincoln says "of," "by" and "for" the people. What do you think each part means?

check.q: What does the Greek word demos mean?
check.why: The reading says demos means the people and kratos means power.

check.q: In a democracy, what can happen to a leader who does a poor job?
choices: The leader can be voted out
check.why: The reading says leaders who do a poor job can be voted out.

check.q: What is a ballot?
choices: The paper or screen where you mark your choice
check.why: The reading defines a ballot as the paper or screen where you mark your choice.

lessons.title: Power Without Fair Votes
lessons.mainIdea: In a dictatorship, one person or a small group holds power without fair elections.
reading: Imagine a country where the leader's picture hangs in every classroom. Newspapers may only say good things about him. People who complain can be arrested. There is an election, but only one name is on the ballot.
This kind of government is a *dictatorship*. One person or a small group holds all the power. The leader is called a *dictator*. There are no fair elections, so people cannot vote the leader out.

Dictators often say they keep the country strong and safe. But people in dictatorships often lose rights, like the right to speak freely. Many people who lived under dictators later worked hard to bring in fair votes.

words.d: a government where one person or small group holds power without fair votes
a leader who holds power without being fairly chosen by the people

look.title: Spot the Difference
look.text: Country A: Three people run for leader. Newspapers write about all of them. Everyone over 18 votes in secret. Country B: One person runs for leader. Newspapers must praise him. Soldiers watch people vote.
look.prompt: Which country has fair elections? Name two clues that helped you decide.

check.q: Who holds power in a dictatorship?
choices: One person or a small group
check.why: The reading says one person or a small group holds all the power.

check.q: Which clue from the reading shows an election is not fair?
choices: Only one name on the ballot
check.why: The reading describes an election with only one name on the ballot as unfair.

check.q: What right do people often lose under a dictator?
check.why: The reading says people in dictatorships often lose rights like speaking freely.

lessons.title: Athens Tries Something New
lessons.mainIdea: Ancient Athens was one of the first democracies, but only some people could vote.
reading: About 2,500 years ago, the city of Athens in Greece tried a new idea. Around 508 BCE, a leader named Cleisthenes helped give power to the citizens. Citizens met on a hill called the Pnyx. They listened to speeches and raised their hands to vote.
This was *direct democracy*. Citizens voted on laws themselves, not through leaders. Athens is often called one of the first democracies in the world. People today still study its ideas.

But not everyone in Athens could vote. Only free men born to Athenian families were *citizens* with a vote. Women could not vote. Enslaved people and people from other places could not vote either. So many people had no say.

words.d: a democracy where citizens vote on laws themselves
a member of a country or city who has rights there, such as voting

look.title: Pericles Praises Athens
look.text: Our government is called a democracy because power is in the hands of the many, not the few. Everyone is equal under the law.
look.cite: Pericles, Funeral Oration, as recorded by Thucydides in History of the Peloponnesian War, c. 400 BCE
look.prompt: Pericles says power belongs to "the many." Based on the reading, who was left out of "the many"?

check.q: Where did Athens citizens meet to vote?
choices: On a hill called the Pnyx
check.why: The reading says citizens met on a hill called the Pnyx.

check.q: What is direct democracy?
choices: Leaders are chosen by a coin toss
check.why: The reading says in direct democracy citizens vote on laws themselves.

check.q: Who could NOT vote in ancient Athens?
check.why: The reading says women, enslaved people and people from other places could not vote.

lessons.title: Choosing Representatives
lessons.mainIdea: In a representative democracy, people elect a smaller group to make laws for them.
reading: Athens was one city. The United States has over 300 million people. They cannot all meet on one hill! So Americans do something different. They choose people to make laws for them.

A person chosen to speak and vote for others is a *representative*. Choosing them is called an *election*. Illinois voters elect people to the U.S. Congress in Washington, D.C. Those lawmakers vote on laws for the whole country.

This is called representative democracy. Most democracies today work this way. Supporters say it lets busy people have a say. Critics say representatives do not always do what voters want. Voters can choose someone new next time.

words.d: a person chosen to speak and vote for a group of people
a time when people vote to choose leaders

look.title: How Many Lawmakers?
look.cite: U.S. House of Representatives and U.S. Senate websites; UK Parliament website
look.prompt: Which group has the most members? Why might a big country need hundreds of lawmakers?

check.q: Why can't all Americans meet on one hill to vote on laws?
check.why: The reading says the United States has over 300 million people, too many to meet in one place.

check.q: What is a representative?
choices: A person chosen to speak and vote for others
check.why: The reading defines a representative as a person chosen to speak and vote for others.

check.q: Look at the chart. How many members does the U.S. Senate have?
check.why: The chart shows the U.S. Senate has 100 members.

lessons.title: Kings and Queens Today
lessons.mainIdea: In a constitutional monarchy, a king or queen remains, but elected leaders make the laws.
reading: In 2023, King Charles III was crowned in London. There were golden coaches and a crown. But King Charles does not make the laws of the United Kingdom. A group of elected lawmakers called Parliament does that.
The UK is a *constitutional monarchy*. It still has a monarch. But a set of rules limits the monarch's power. A written or unwritten plan for how a government works is called a *constitution*.

Japan and Spain are also constitutional monarchies. Japan has an emperor, Naruhito. Spain has a king, Felipe VI. In each country, people vote for the leaders who run the government. The monarch stands for the nation's history and unity.

words.d: a country with a king or queen whose power is limited, where elected leaders make laws
the basic plan and rules for how a government works

look.title: Japan's Emperor as a Symbol
look.text: The Emperor is the symbol of the country and of the unity of its people. His place comes from the will of the people.
look.prompt: The emperor is called a symbol. What is the difference between being a symbol and making the laws?

check.q: Who makes the laws in the United Kingdom today?
choices: Parliament, a group of elected lawmakers
check.why: The reading says Parliament, not the king, makes the UK's laws.

check.q: Which country is a constitutional monarchy?
check.why: The reading names the UK, Japan and Spain as constitutional monarchies.

check.q: What is a constitution?
choices: The basic plan and rules for how a government works
check.why: The reading says a constitution is a plan for how a government works.

lessons.title: Countries With No King
lessons.mainIdea: A republic has no monarch; its leaders are chosen, often by the people's votes.
reading: In 1776, American leaders signed the Declaration of Independence. They broke away from the British king. They did not want a new king. Instead, they built a *republic*, a country with no monarch.

In a republic, the head of the country is chosen, not born into the job. In the United States, voters choose a *president* every four years. France, Mexico and India are republics too. Each one has a president.

Republics work in different ways. In the U.S. and Mexico, the president leads the government. In India, a prime minister leads it, and the president has a smaller role. But in all of them, no family owns the top job.

words.d: a country with no king or queen, where leaders are chosen
the chosen head of a republic

look.title: When Some Republics Began
look.prompt: Which of these republics is the oldest? Which is the newest? How many years apart are they?

check.q: What makes a country a republic?
choices: It has no monarch and its leaders are chosen
check.why: The reading says a republic is a country with no monarch, where leaders are chosen.

check.q: How often do U.S. voters choose a president?
check.why: The reading says U.S. voters choose a president every four years.

check.q: In India, who leads the government?
check.why: The reading says in India a prime minister leads the government.

review.q: Which kind of government is ruled by a king or queen?
review.why: A monarchy is ruled by a king or queen, called a monarch.

review.q: What do governments use tax money for?
choices: Paying for public services like roads and schools
review.why: Taxes pay for public services that everyone shares.

review.q: Which city is known as one of the first democracies?
review.why: Ancient Athens began its democracy around 508 BCE.

review.q: How is a dictatorship different from a democracy?
choices: In a dictatorship, people choose laws directly
In a dictatorship, people cannot fairly vote the leader out
review.why: Dictatorships have no fair elections, while democracies let people vote leaders out.

review.q: Spain has a king, but elected leaders make the laws. What kind of government is this?
review.why: In a constitutional monarchy, a monarch remains but elected leaders make laws.

review.q: Which country is a republic with a president?
review.why: Mexico is a republic; the UK, Japan and Spain have monarchs.

review.q: In a representative democracy, what do voters do?
choices: Elect people to make laws for them
review.why: Voters elect representatives to make laws for them.

review.q: Who helps settle a disagreement about whether a law was broken?
review.why: A court is where a judge listens to both sides and decides.
